chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-A'lawi, from al-'Umari, from Ali ibn Ja'far, from his brother Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), said:

I asked him about a Muslim man who has a Jewish or Christian female slave under his ownership, and he fathers a child by her and accuses her (of adultery). Is there li'an (mutual imprecation) upon him? He said: No. The basis in his saying (peace be upon him): 'No, at the questioner's asking whether li'an is upon him,' is one of two things: One is that he returns to the denial of the child, so it is held that if he acknowledges the child and then denies it, his denial is not heeded, the child is established as his, and li'an does not occur between them. And if we say that he returns to the accusation (of adultery), then li'an does not occur between them merely by the accusation, according to what we have previously established, until he adds to it the claim of witnessing (the act).

key_terms.الْمُعَايَنَة: Witnessing (the act of adultery), a condition for certain legal rulings regarding li'an.
key_terms.قَذْفَ: Accusation of adultery (zina) without four witnesses.
key_terms.لِعَانٌ: Li'an (mutual imprecation), a specific legal procedure in Islamic jurisprudence where husband and wife accuse each other of adultery and deny paternity, resulting in the severing of lineage.

ai.seo_question: Does li'an apply to a Muslim man who fathers a child with his non-Muslim female slave?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Istibsar clarifies that li'an (mutual imprecation) does not apply between a free Muslim man and his non-Muslim female slave, a ruling derived from Imam al-Sadiq (AS). The text distinguishes between denying paternity, which is not accepted if followed by acknowledgment, and accusing of adultery, which requires a claim of eyewitness testimony to trigger li'an. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance that the formal ritual of li'an is contingent on specific conditions of accusation and witness, rather than mere paternity disputes.
